description: GENERATED by scripts/assessment/readings.py from evidence-map.json: the reviewer's strict reading. Map from ETSI EN 303 645 provisions that a Model N observer can show violated (E3, fail_only) — plus the one pass_only provision — to the Quarant signals that would carry that evidence. status: implemented = the signal is the violation evidence (under the stated assumptions); candidate_only = the signal finds candidates but cannot confirm the violation; not_implemented = no Quarant signal yet.

provisions.violation_evidence: A non-user-defined password seen in cleartext equals a published universal default.
provisions.gap: Values are masked by design; no comparison against published default-credential lists.
provisions.audit: Tokens are not passwords; only password-bearing evidence counts. 2026-10-21 (D27): added from the Zeek path; awaiting the user's review of the mapping. An SNMP agent answering public/private (compared in memory) is direct evidence of a universal default credential being accepted.

provisions.violation_evidence: A pre-installed password seen in cleartext is weak or derived from public data (MAC, SSID).
provisions.gap: Same as 5.1-1; password strength is not assessed.
provisions.audit: 2026-10-21 (D27): added from the Zeek path; awaiting the user's review of the mapping. An SNMP agent answering public/private (compared in memory) is direct evidence of a universal default credential being accepted.

provisions.violation_evidence: The device authenticates to a service with a password (machine-to-machine), visible in cleartext.
provisions.filter: device is the client and the server is external
provisions.audit: E4 sample: 0/15 INSECURE_HTTP_AUTH events were M2M password logins (13 x-token headers, 2 user Basic logins to the device).

provisions.violation_evidence: Authentication runs over cryptography outside the best-practice catalogue (e.g. TLS 1.0/1.1, weak suites selected).
provisions.audit: E4 sample: weak version 15/15 correct; all 15 'weak cipher selected' were CBC suites, which are not violation evidence by themselves, so only broken suites count. E6 (CIC 2022 power-on): 4/4 devices correct. Nest Cam, Netatmo camera and Hue bridge offered at most TLS 1.0 themselves; Echo Spot offered TLS 1.2 and a video-service server selected TLS 1.0. E11/E12: two 2016 misses fixed: a camera serving TLS that chose TLS 1.0 for a phone offering 1.2 (finding now goes to the server), and a blood-pressure meter on port 8777 whose first segment held only the record header. 2026-10-21 (D27): added from the Zeek path; awaiting the user's review of the mapping. Certificates: leaf key under NIST SP 800-131A minimums or SHA-1/MD5 signature (not for self-signed). SSH: SSH-1, RFC 9142 SHOULD NOT/MUST NOT key exchange, RC4 (RFC 8758) or none cipher.

provisions.violation_evidence: Third-party password guessing against the device is answered without delay or lockout.
provisions.gap: Only RTSP is examined. Continued 401 answers cannot be told apart from a lockout that also answers 401, so a run of failures is a candidate; only success_after_failures=true shows the failures did not lock the client out. Reporting marks runs beyond the NIST SP 800-63B limit of 100 consecutive failures.
provisions.audit: E9 (CIC 2022 RTSP brute force): SimCam answered ~3,500 Hydra attempts per run (~23/s) with 401 and no refusal; Amcrest answered 36 with 401. No run ended in success, so neither is confirmed.

provisions.violation_evidence: The observed firmware version is affected by a public CVE long after a fix was disclosed.
provisions.gap: The version a device names (HTTP Server, SSH banner, DHCP vendor class) is matched against NVD affected ranges, counting only CVEs published before the capture. The named version may not be the one running, vendors backport fixes without changing the version string, and the affected feature may not be built in (BusyBox applets). How long counts as 'timely' is not decided; the evidence gives the days since publication.
provisions.audit: 2026-10-21 (D28): added from the Zeek path; awaiting the user's review of the mapping.

provisions.violation_evidence: (pass evidence) An update is installed without user action.
provisions.gap: Whether the user triggered the update is not known.

provisions.violation_evidence: Software updates are delivered over cleartext or weak cryptography.
provisions.assumption: the HTTP transfer is a software update (keyword-based)
provisions.gap: Cleartext transport of an update does not show weak update cryptography: the package may be signed (TS 5.3-7 concerns the update mechanism's cryptography).
provisions.audit: E4 sample: transfers were plausibly updates (path contains 'ota'); signature status unknown.

provisions.violation_evidence: A device function reachable over the network is served without authentication.
provisions.assumption: the function is not meant as open access inside the home network (EN 303 645 5.5-4 itself allows services made available without authentication within a restricted network, e.g. DLNA)
provisions.gap: Authentication outside the request (earlier pairing, host allow-lists, a physical button) is not visible; whether the function was carried out is not known.
provisions.audit: E5: IoT devices with evidence: 2016 HP printer (status queries on 3910/3911 and IPP printing from a PC answered without credentials; one unauthenticated PUT of /DevMgmt/ProductConfigDyn.xml), 2018 Belkin WeMo (GetHomeInfo SOAP answered 200 without credentials). Printer status and printing may fall under the restricted-network exception; the configuration write and the WeMo call do not obviously. Most matches overall were the gateway's UPnP IGD (non-IoT, excluded). E6 (CIC 2022 power-on): the only match was a DLNA GetProtocolInfo to a Sonos MediaRenderer, which EN 303 645 5.5-4 itself cites as an allowed restricted-network service; DLNA/UPnP AV services are excluded.

provisions.violation_evidence: A security-relevant configuration change is performed over the network without authentication.
Critical security parameters (credentials, tokens) travel in cleartext or over weak cryptography.
provisions.audit: E4 sample: HTTP auth/token headers 15/15 and session IDs in URLs 4/4 correct; 4/4 'token' events were device serial numbers (identifiers, not CSPs) and are excluded; cookies may be non-session (probable). IoT-23: a Philips Hue sent Authorization headers and auth= URL parameters in cleartext to its cloud (correct). E6 (CIC 2022 power-on): Hue bridge (Authorization headers, auth= in URL) and Home Eye camera (Authorization header) to cloud over HTTP, both correct. E8 (CIC 2022 interactions/scenarios): Hue bridge again (correct); a Sonos One sent sid= in cleartext URLs to opml.radiotime.com (TuneIn radio session ID; whether it is a critical security parameter is unclear, undecided). E9 (CIC 2022 active): SimCam's Authorization headers to S3 were AWS SigV4 signatures (per-request, not reusable), now named in the evidence and excluded; the same requests uploaded JPEG snapshots in cleartext, which is 5.8-1 evidence Quarant does not yet detect. E11 (miss measurement): INSECURE_HTTP_BODY_SECRET was missing from this list; across all data its IoT events outside the serial=/device_id= exclusion were Withings sessionid= (4 devices) and an iHome evrythng.api_key= (all correct), so it is now included. INSECURE_MQTT_PAYLOAD_SECRET and INSECURE_TELNET_PAYLOAD_SECRET never occurred and stay out (unaudited). Home Eye's Authorization was an Alibaba OSS per-request signature (false positive); OSS and WSSE are now named in the evidence and excluded like AWS SigV4. E14 (YourThings 2018, unseen devices): two misses, a VeraLite hub logging into an external FTP server in cleartext and a Harmony Hub receiving an API key in a cleartext HTTP response; INSECURE_FTP_CREDENTIALS and INSECURE_HTTP_RESPONSE_SECRET were added afterwards. 2026-10-21 (D27): added from the Zeek path; awaiting the user's review of the mapping. SNMP v1/v2c communities accepted by an agent travel in cleartext.

provisions.violation_evidence: Critical security parameters cross remotely accessible interfaces in cleartext.
provisions.filter: peer is external (the source or the destination is a public address)
provisions.audit: 2026-10-21 (D27): added from the Zeek path; awaiting the user's review of the mapping. SNMP v1/v2c communities accepted by an agent travel in cleartext.

provisions.violation_evidence: Unauthenticated discovery or banner traffic discloses software versions that the protocol does not require.
provisions.assumption: the disclosed version is security-relevant and not needed for operation
provisions.gap: Most visible version strings are mandated by the protocol (UPnP SERVER header) or are protocol versions (mDNS pv=, vers=); TS 5.6-2 itself notes that standard protocols may require such disclosure.
provisions.audit: E4 sample: 0/22 discovery version strings were evidence of a violation. 2026-10-21 (D28): added from the Zeek path; awaiting the user's review of the mapping. Versions in HTTP Server headers, FTP greetings and the DHCP vendor class are not required by those protocols; SSH banners and the UPnP SERVER string are, and are left at low confidence or out.

provisions.violation_evidence: Personal data is sent to associated services in cleartext.
provisions.audit: E4 sample: 10/10 correct (user identifier in cleartext body); all from one device. E10 (I6_MEDIA_UPLOAD_CLEARTEXT): all matches checked. Home Eye camera PUT JPEG snapshots to Alibaba Cloud OSS (Hong Kong) over HTTP at power-on (3/3), on 14/30 idle nights and in the active day; SimCam PUT JPEGs to S3 over HTTP. Both correct. No match in UNSW 2016/2018 or IoT-23; a direct search of the raw traffic of three UNSW days found no media upload either. E11/E12: the rule read only the first multipart part and missed a 2016 TP-Link camera streaming h264 video and AAC audio to tplinkcloud.com over HTTP (now every part is read); a Borun camera (CIC 2022 power-on) sent JPEGs inside a proprietary TCP protocol to port 8899 (now detected by file signature, device to public address only). E4's 2018 match was a MacBook Pro, not an IoT device.

provisions.violation_evidence: Sensitive personal data is sent in cleartext.
provisions.gap: No distinction between personal and sensitive personal data.

provisions.violation_evidence: After a natural outage the device does not reconnect.
Reconnection is disorderly (tight retry loops, no backoff).
provisions.gap: Backoff and protocol conformance are not checked.
provisions.audit: E4 sample: 0/12 PERSISTENT_CONNECTION_ATTEMPTS were reconnect storms (all answered, regular sessions); only mostly-unanswered retry loops count. IoT-23: the 3 mostly-unanswered loops were malware C2/scan loops, i.e. infection behaviour rather than the product's reconnection design; traffic alone cannot separate the two. E7 (CIC 2022 idle): Borun camera retried logreport.nvcam.net:80 about 40 times an hour, mostly unanswered, on many nights (a retry loop against an unresponsive logging server: plausible, backoff not checked); SimCam once.

provisions.violation_evidence: User identifiers still appear in traffic after a user reset.
Insecure defaults are visible out of the box (cleartext management services answering, UPnP port mappings).
provisions.gap: Default vs user-enabled is not known (applies to listening services and to UPnP port mappings alike).
provisions.audit: E5: one IoT device (2018 Belkin NetCam) repeatedly mapped external TCP 9031 to itself through UPnP and the gateway accepted; the other mappings came from a PC and an Android phone (excluded).

provisions.violation_evidence: Malformed inbound input is followed by a crash or error leak.
Identifiable data appears in cleartext uploads of data meant to be anonymised.
provisions.gap: Which data should be anonymised is not known under Model N.
